1. A small study reports “not statistically significant”, and adds that its observed power was 30%. Explain why this does not show there is no real effect, and why the observed power adds no information. What should the authors report instead?

Failing to reject H₀ is not proving it (§8.1). A small study has a large standard error, so it can miss a real, clinically important effect (a Type II error). The “observed power” is power computed at the observed effect: Φ(|z| − 1.96), a one-to-one function of the p-value. Every result with p > 0.05 has observed power below about 50%, so “30%” only restates “p was well above 0.05” (Hoenig & Heisey, 2001). The authors should report the effect estimate with its 95% confidence interval. If the interval includes clinically important effects, the study is inconclusive, not negative. Power belongs to the planning stage, for an effect size chosen in advance.

2. Explain the trade-off between Type I and Type II error using a clinical example of your choosing. What, besides a larger sample, could reduce both?

Example: testing a new antihypertensive against H₀ “no effect”. A Type I error approves a useless drug; a Type II error abandons a useful one. For a fixed sample and design, lowering α (say from 0.05 to 0.01) moves the critical values outwards: fewer false approvals, more missed effects (in §8.4 power for a true 1 kg difference fell from 0.69 to 0.46). Both errors fall only if the standard error falls. Besides a larger n, a paired or matched design (each person as their own control) or a more precise measurement (less variability) lowers the SE and so reduces both.

3. For the urban–rural comparison (SE_diff = 0.406 kg, pooled SD 1.891 kg), compute the standardised effect size d and the power for a true difference of 0.5 kg. How many children per group (σ = 2 kg, z-formula) would give 80% power for 0.5 kg?

d = 0.5/1.891 = 0.26.

Power ≈ Φ(Δ/SE − 1.96) = Φ(0.5/0.406 − 1.96) = Φ(1.232 − 1.96) = Φ(−0.73) = 0.23. The study would miss a true 0.5 kg difference about 77% of the time.

n per group = 2(1.96 + 0.84)²σ²/Δ² = 2 × 7.84 × 4/0.25 = 250.9 → 251 per group (with the unrounded z-values, 1.95996 and 0.84162, 251.2 → 252; the t-distribution version, which software computes, gives 252.1 → 253). Halving the effect to be detected quadruples n (63 → about 251).

1. Two studies report p = 0.001 and p = 0.049. A colleague says the first is “much more significant”, so its effect must be larger. What is right and what is wrong in this?

Right: both are below 0.05, and the smaller p does indicate greater incompatibility of that study’s data with H₀ under its statistical model. Wrong: (1) “significant” at α = 0.05 is a yes/no classification, and both studies cross it; (2) a p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect (ASA, 2016, principle 5). A tiny effect in a very large study can give p = 0.001, and a large effect in a small study p = 0.049. To compare effects, look at each study’s effect estimate with its confidence interval.

2. A trial tests a new drug in 8 independent subgroups, each at α = 0.05, and the drug truly does nothing. What is the probability of at least one “significant” subgroup? What per-test threshold would Bonferroni use?

Family-wise error rate = 1 − (1 − 0.05)⁸ = 1 − 0.95⁸ = 1 − 0.663 = 0.337: about one chance in three of a false “finding”. Bonferroni tests each subgroup at 0.05/8 = 0.00625.

3. A district sample of 100 births has mean birthweight 2.9 kg. Test H₀: μ = 3.0 kg with σ = 0.5 kg: compute z and the two-sided p. The team, seeing the result lies below 3.0 kg, switches to a one-tailed test. What p would they report, and why is the switch wrong?

SE = 0.5/√100 = 0.05 kg. z = (2.9 − 3.0)/0.05 = −2.00. Two-sided p = 2 × [1 − Φ(2.00)] = 0.046. One-tailed (H₁: μ < 3.0) p = 0.023, half the two-sided value. The switch is wrong because the direction was chosen after seeing the data. It halves the p-value. A team that picks the tail the data point to, then tests at 0.05, rejects whenever the two-sided p is below 0.10, so its real Type I error rate is 10%, not the 5% it claims. This is p-hacking (§8.6). The direction must be fixed at step 1, before the data are seen. Note also that H₀ here is μ = 3.0 kg, not “no effect”.

1. Name the five questions you ask to choose a statistical test, and say why the design question comes first.

  1. Type of outcome (quantitative normal or skewed, ordinal, binary, categorical, count/rate, time to event). (2) What is compared (one group vs a value, two groups, more than two, association of two variables). (3) Independent, paired/matched, or clustered observations. (4) For quantitative outcomes, whether parametric assumptions are reasonable. (5) The study design. The design comes first because it fixes which effect measures are valid: a case-control study, for example, can give only the odds ratio of exposure, never prevalence or risk (§1.5). No choice of test can recover a measure the design cannot supply.

2. Using Tables 8.1–8.4, choose the test and the adjusting model for: (a) haemoglobin before and after iron–folic acid in the same 12 women, with skewed differences; (b) a case-control study of neonatal sepsis with each case matched to a neighbourhood control, exposure “home delivery”; (c) full-immunisation coverage compared between urban and rural children in a 30-cluster survey.

  1. Quantitative, two paired measurements, skewed differences: the sign test (§10.1.1). The Wilcoxon signed-rank test (§10.3) needs roughly symmetric differences, so it fits only if the skew is mild. No regression is needed for a single before–after comparison; to adjust, model the differences (linear regression after transformation, §9.4) or use a mixed model (§15.2.4).
  2. Binary exposure, matched case-control pairs: matched-pair odds ratio b/c and McNemar’s test (§10.8); adjusting model: conditional logistic regression (§13.2.9).
  3. Binary outcome, two groups, clustered sample: difference or ratio of proportions (§10.6.4) with an SE corrected for clustering by the design effect (§6.2.6) or a survey analysis (§15.2.6); adjusting model: logistic regression with GEE or survey weights and PSUs (§15.2.5, §15.2.6). An ordinary chi-square would give a p-value that is too small.

3. In a cohort, 30 of 150 exposed and 15 of 150 unexposed people develop the outcome. Following the seven steps of §8.7, compute the risk difference, the pooled SE under H₀, z and the two-sided p, and the 95% CI of the difference (unpooled SE). State the conclusion.

  1. H₀: risk exposed = risk unexposed; H₁: they differ (two-tailed).
  2. α = 0.05.
  3. Binary outcome, two independent groups → two-proportion z-test (or chi-square). Pooled risk 45/300 = 0.15; under H₀ each group expects 150 × 0.15 = 22.5 events and 127.5 non-events, ample for the normal approximation (§5.7.2.2.4).
  4. Risks 30/150 = 0.20 and 15/150 = 0.10; risk difference = 0.10. SE₀ = √[0.15 × 0.85 × (1/150 + 1/150)] = √(0.1275 × 0.01333) = √0.0017 = 0.0412. z = 0.10/0.0412 = 2.43.
  5. Two-sided p = 2 × [1 − Φ(2.43)] = 0.015.
  6. 0.015 < 0.05: reject H₀.
  7. Unpooled SE = √(0.20 × 0.80/150 + 0.10 × 0.90/150) = √(0.001067 + 0.000600) = 0.0408. 95% CI = 0.10 ± 1.96 × 0.0408 = 0.10 ± 0.080 = 0.020 to 0.180. Conclusion: the risk was 10 percentage points higher in the exposed (20% vs 10%; 95% CI 2.0 to 18.0 points; p = 0.015). The interval is wide: the data are compatible with a small (2 points) or a large (18 points) excess risk. It is an association; confounding has not been addressed.
